$comment: The brand, as data — REQ-049 (#208), task #218. Read by scripts/check-brand.mjs and by the site's CSS. One place, so three approximations of one brand cannot drift apart.

navy.role: The primary. Light-mode links, headings, the mark's centre.
navy.why: The identity that already existed rather than a new one — the same navy the organisation's documents use. A rebrand nobody asked for is a cost with no benefit.

blue.role: The accent. The mark's attendant dots, an active state, a chart's first series.
blue.why: One step lighter than the primary rather than a second hue: the mark reads as one object in two tones, and a second hue would make it read as two things.

sky.why: The navy fails contrast on a dark ground — 2.2:1, unreadable. Not an inversion: a lighter tone of the same hue, chosen for the ratio rather than derived from it.

ink.role: Light-mode body text, and the dark-mode ground.
ink.why: Not #000. A slight navy bias means the neutral belongs to the palette rather than sitting beside it.

slate.why: A grey with the same hue bias as the ink. A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered.

wash.role: A light surface: a callout, a code block, a table header.
wash.why: Tinted rather than #f5f5f5, for the same reason as the slate.

duskInk.why: Not pure white on near-black: 21:1 is harsh at body size, and the eye reads long prose more comfortably a step down.

duskWash.why: Lighter than the dark ground rather than darker: a surface that recedes behind its page is a surface nobody sees.

contrast.use: a link inside a callout, light
a link inside a callout, dark

display.stack: "Iowan Old Style", "Palatino Linotype", Palatino, "Book Antiqua", Georgia, serif
display.role: Headings, the wordmark, a pull quote.
display.why: A transitional serif, because the subject is infrastructure documentation and a serif says 'read this' where a geometric sans says 'scroll past it'. Iowan and Palatino are on macOS and Windows respectively; Georgia is everywhere, so the last resort is still a considered face rather than the browser's default.

body.stack: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif
body.why: The system face, deliberately. See `webfont` below.

mono.stack: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, "SF Mono", Menlo, Consolas, "Liberation Mono", monospace
mono.role: Code, identifiers, anything a reader might retype.

webfont.why: AC-7 says nothing renders from a URL we do not control, and a Google Fonts stylesheet is exactly that: a third party learning every reader's IP address, and a page whose type shifts when their CDN is slow. Self-hosting would need a licensed file committed here, which is a decision about money and licences rather than about design. A system pairing is a real pairing — it has a serif for display and a sans for body — and it costs one fewer request than any alternative.

scale.why: Seven steps, roughly a minor third. Enough for a document; few enough that a heading level is a decision rather than a guess.

measure.why: Running text near 65–70 characters. Wider and the eye loses the line return; the default in a wide browser window is nearly twice this.

mark.why: Below about 20px the attendant dots merge into the centre and it reads as a blob. Use the centre circle alone if you need smaller.

clearSpace.value: half the mark's height on every side
clearSpace.why: The sweep's open gap is the mark's distinguishing feature, and it disappears when something is set against it.

onColour.value: the mark's own two tones on paper or ink only
onColour.why: It is a two-tone mark, so it has no single-colour form yet. Setting it on the accent blue leaves the dots invisible.

wordmark.value: not production-ready — the type is <text>, not paths
wordmark.why: The letter shapes render with whatever font the viewer has, so the same file looks different on two machines. Outlining against a licensed face is the last step before public use, and the name was not settled when the marks were drawn.
